item.title: Guam Board of Education chair wants oversight hearing on Public Health's requirements for schools
item.description: Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division. Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms
item.content:encoded:
Guam Board of Education Chairperson Judith Guthertz said Monday she would like the chair of the Legislature’s Committee on Education to call an immediate oversight hearing for the Department of Public Health’s Environmental Health Division.

Guthertz said she was upset because people on a radio talk show were making fun of the Education Department for installing air conditioning in school restrooms, but the department is merely complying with Public Health regulations.

She said the oversight hearing should be called, “with the goal of determining whether or not these regulations make sense. That is the source of many of the difficulties that we have experienced over the last few months.”

The Tiyan High School campus, which also housed students from Simon Sanchez High School, was closed by Public Health shortly after the school year began in August, leading to double sessions and emergency repairs.

She wanted the public to know the idea for cooler bathrooms did not come from the Education Department.

“People in the community don't understand this, that we have to honor those regulations, no matter whether or not they make sense,” she said, questioning whether air conditioning in restrooms would affect student learning. “I take great exception to the lack of clarification on the part of the media that do not understand where these regulations come from.”

She said air conditioning is also being installed at University of Guam restrooms.

“Can you imagine what the costs are going to be for DOE? We have to do this in every school, in every bathroom, and at the university and at GCC. Why could we not put ceiling fans? Would that not help?” she asked. “Split units, the cost of retrofitting the electrical requirements, the installation costs, the material costs, the equipment costs. I'd rather use that money in the classrooms.”

Because the matter could not be addressed during Monday’s emergency meeting for the department’s spending plan, Guthertz asked that it be placed on the board agenda for the upcoming Nov. 17 meeting.

The board will consider whether to ask the superintendent to request an oversight hearing on the Public Health requirements.

item.title: DPW announces Simon Sanchez High School project to move forward through two separate procurement processes
item.description: The Department of Public Works announced that the Simon Sanchez High School project is moving forward through two separate procurement processes, but neither demolition nor construction has officially begun. Under the first procurement process, Public Works has completed its part of the bidding process for demolishing the existing Simon Sanchez High School Campus, and the Office of the Attorney Ge
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Works announced that the Simon Sanchez High School project is moving forward through two separate procurement processes, but neither demolition nor construction has officially begun.

Under the first procurement process, Public Works has completed its part of the bidding process for demolishing the existing Simon Sanchez High School Campus, and the Office of the Attorney General has reviewed and cleared the demolition bid documents. However, Public Works is still waiting for GDOE to authorize the architect, TRMA, to finish the remaining work and release the documents needed. Once GDOE accepts, Public Works says it is ready to advertise the demolition bidding and move forward.

For the second procurement and the construction of the new school, Public Works has completed preparing the request for proposals for the school’s construction through a public-private partnership. The proposal package still needs final review by the Attorney General's Office before it is issued. Public Works plans to turn over the procurement package to the incoming administration for consideration and implementation.

item.title: Selection committee to interview six MVA director candidates
item.description: The Marianas Visitors Authority board of directors has formed a selection committee to evaluate six applicants for the agency's vacant managing director position. The action came during a special board meeting Monday where directors addressed the recently closed job vacancy announcement for MVA's top executive post.
item.content:encoded:
The Marianas Visitors Authority board of directors has formed a selection committee to evaluate six applicants for the agency's vacant managing director position.

The action came during a special board meeting Monday where directors addressed the recently closed job vacancy announcement for MVA's top executive post.

Acting Managing Director Judy Torres told board members that the application period ended last week.

The board approved the creation of a selection committee tasked with reviewing applications, conducting interviews and recommending a candidate to the full board.

The committee consists of board members Sakuro Gerrard, Chris Nelson and Joe Guerrero, along with Torres and MVA Human Resources Manager Tina Matsunaga.

Acting Board Chair Vicky Benavente said the committee will begin its work as soon as possible.

"The selection committee will meet as soon as possible and conduct interviews and evaluations and will make a recommendation to the whole board," Benavente said.

Speaking with reporters following the meeting, Torres declined to identify the applicants.

Asked whether MVA has established a target date for hiring its next managing director, Torres said the timeline will depend on how quickly the committee can complete its review process.

"It all depends on how soon the committee can review the applications and set up a date to proceed," she said.

No timeline for a final hiring decision was announced.

item.content:encoded:
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — When Ueno Bank's services abruptly stopped working in the early hours of Tuesday morning , the consequences were immediate for the millions of Paraguayans who had come to depend on it for everyday transactions.

"People don't have any trust," said Elizabeth González, a 28-year-old barista at a café in downtown Asunción, a few blocks from Paraguay's Congress building, where protesters had begun gathering after the bank's collapse was announced Tuesday.

Earlier, one customer had walked into the café and insisted on paying in cash. He no longer trusted any bank.

"If Paraguayans themselves aren't confident right now, foreign investors will be less so," González said.

The collapse affected far more than the bank's shareholders. Ueno said it had 2.9 million customers — around 60% of Paraguay's adult population. The Central Bank said the bank had approximately 1.8 million depositors.

By Saturday, authorities said almost 1.2 million customers had received an advance payment under the state's deposit guarantee fund, but many were still waiting.

It also led to the impeachment and removal of President Santiago Peña, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and exposed a power struggle inside within the ruling Colorado Party.

The anger was palpable outside Congress on Friday, where hundreds had gathered to protest not only their inability to access their money but also what they saw as a broader failure of accountability.

"I came not because it affects me personally, but because it affects all of Paraguay," said Elodia Saveredo, a 71-year-old housewife who sells her own handicrafts online.

Batarram Caballero, a 23-year-old fifth-year biochemistry student and president of the student center at the National University of Asunción, said classmates had money frozen that they needed to cover basic expenses.

"It wasn't a lot of money, perhaps, but it was money for their bus fare. It was money for their food," she said. "To hear that and not be able to do anything because I don't have the resources to help them is very discouraging."

Ueno Bank launched as a fintech in 2021 and began operating as a bank in November 2023 . Its meteoric rise to become one of the country's most important financial institutions was driven by slick marketing and a digital model based around convenience and cashback deals; customers could open accounts on their phones and were offered incentives to process payments through the platform.

Caballero believes the crisis was foretold by an intense campaign in the days before accounts were frozen.

"They were bombarding us with messages telling us to put our money there," she said. "There were also rumors about what was already on the cards."

The bank also held substantial public funds. The Social Security Institute, known as IPS, had around $355 million invested in Ueno, roughly 9% of its portfolio.

The sums involved have raised questions about how such a young bank came to hold so much public money.

Manuel Ferreira, an economist and former finance minister, told local outlet ABC Color that the collapse raised fundamental questions about how the bank managed its assets. He pointed out that, in a typical bank, shareholders provide only a small portion of the money behind its assets, while the bulk comes from customer deposits.

He also argued that marketing and discounts helped attract customers but did not create lasting assets. A bank's principal asset, he said, was its loan portfolio: money owed by borrowers.

But in the case of Ueno, many of those loans had gone to companies directly linked to the bank's controlling owners, Grupo Vásquez, including $146 million in loans made to just three companies. He described Ueno's promissory notes as being signed by the same people on both sides of some transactions.

The scandal hit Peña particularly hard because of his personal links to the bank's holding company, in which he held shares even after taking up the presidency. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, who had led Ueno Bank, to head Paraguay's Central Bank in 2023.

In his asset declaration submitted weeks after taking up the presidency in 2023, Peña listed shares in Ueno Holding, then valued at around $845,000. Those shares represented around 1.6% of the company's paid-up capital when he later sold them in March 2025.

Prosecutors allege that, while president, he used his position to influence public agencies and state-owned entities to maintain deposits with the bank despite his connections to its parent group.

Peña resigned Thursday and was impeached and removed from office Friday. The following day, prosecutors charged him with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. He was ordered held in pretrial detention at a military facility pending the investigation. Peña has pleaded not guilty. Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, has been sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028.

Carvallo was also arrested and charged with breach of trust, administration for personal gain and producing false public documents. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a police facility. Eight Ueno executives, including 36-year-old CEO Miguel Vásquez, were also arrested and charged.

The crisis has also put the spotlight on Horacio Cartes, a tobacco magnate and former president of Paraguay who wields considerable political and economic influence.

Cartes handpicked Peña, his former finance minister, to lead his Honor Colorado faction into the 2023 presidential election. But the relationship between the two men had become increasingly strained, apparently over Peña's efforts to establish his own power base within the party.

In September, senators aligned with Cartes sought information from the Central Bank about Ueno's transactions with related companies and its public-sector deposits.

After the bank collapsed, Cartes publicly distanced himself from Peña, releasing a public statement on Wednesday calling for an investigation and insisting there should be "no impunity for anyone." The following day, his faction backed Peña's impeachment.

The move was widely seen as a decisive withdrawal of political protection for Peña, and an opportunity for Cartes to reassert his influence.

But for those gathered outside Congress protesting, the scandal was about more than a bank collapse. It was a reckoning with Paraguay's political establishment.

item.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's alleged relationship with Chinese spy
item.description: The massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia says it is launching an internal investigation, after reports that the company's CEO was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy. In the statement announcing the investigation, Nvidia cited recent reporting by The New York Times , which alleges Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation that sought to send adv
item.content:encoded:
The massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia says it is launching an internal investigation, after reports that the company's CEO was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

In the statement announcing the investigation, Nvidia cited recent reporting by The New York Times , which alleges Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation that sought to send advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the statement from the company's board of directors reads in part.

The Times released a series of reports over the last two weeks detailing Huang's alleged relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, who is accused of being a spy for China. The two are not related. NPR has reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C. but has not received a response.

"Alice Huang is a Chinese national. She's a Chinese businesswoman who had something of a mysterious and meteoric rise," Times reporter Ana Swanson explained on NPR's technology podcast Machine Gods .

Alice Huang ran a Singapore-based company that purchased nearly $5 billion in Nvidia chip technology, Swanson says. "At the same time, she was also seen personally with Jensen Huang on a couple of occasions after some industry events in Taiwan. They were photographed together both at a bar with other suppliers and then also out to dinner with some other executives."

The reporting by the Times suggests Alice Huang may have helped China get around U.S. limits on exports of powerful AI chips.

According to Nvidia, Huang sent an email to his employees on Sunday, acknowledging the relationship, and apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife.

"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," Huang wrote. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

Last week, three Republican members of Congress sent a letter to the Nvidia CEO requesting that he brief lawmakers about the relationship, and about the company's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage."

Nvidia dominates the global market for AI chips, and has seen explosive growth in recent years, as NPR has reported . The company started as a manufacturer of chips for computer graphics, which later turned out to be crucial for training artificial intelligence .

Nvidia's CEO and President Trump have repeatedly appeared in public together in recent years. According to Huang, Nvidia is helping to fund the construction of a new ballroom at the White House.

item.title: NASA is looking for astronauts to live and work on the Moon
item.description: If you have dreams of going to the moon, you now have a chance. NASA is accepting applications for those interested in becoming an astronaut. The candidates selected to be astronauts would not only test spacecraft but would also live and work on the moon in a future moon base, said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a statement released on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
If you have dreams of going to the moon, you now have a chance. NASA is accepting applications for those interested in becoming an astronaut.

The candidates selected to be astronauts would not only test spacecraft but would also live and work on the moon in a future moon base, said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a statement released on Saturday.

"Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage," the statement said. "NASA's astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation."

There are currently 32 active astronauts in NASA's astronaut corps. Since NASA missions began in the 1960s, the agency has selected 370 people to train as astronauts, according to the agency.

The applicant process is extremely competitive. Out of more than 8,000 applicants for NASA's last astronaut class, only 10 candidates were selected.

While any U.S. citizen can apply and there is no official age restriction, applicants will need to have a master's degree in a STEM-related field such as engineering or math.

In a recent change, a nursing degree qualifies.

"Nursing degrees are now included in the STEM definition," Anna Schneider, NASA spokesperson, told NPR on Sunday. "Master's-level nursing degrees now meet the minimum educational requirement, whereas nursing degrees were previously excluded."

In addition, NASA is requiring a minimum of three years of related professional experience after completing a degree.

In lieu of a master's degree and working experience, NASA will consider those in a PhD program (in STEM), doctors or pilots with extensive flight experience.

If chosen, the selected astronauts will undergo training that will last for two years. NASA said astronauts will prepare for critical and difficult missions such as landing near the moon's South Pole.

To achieve its goal of returning humans to the moon in 2028 – the first time since 1972 – NASA is relying on private companies such as Blue Origin and SpaceX to develop systems and spacecraft.

During a Nov. 7 press conference on the Artemis III moon mission's progress, Isaacman said he is "very confident" the mission will launch in 2027.

The starting salary is $164,395 and applications will be received through Dec. 3.

item.content:encoded:
European officials will turn up for the U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates this week, France's foreign minister said Sunday, days after the Kremlin had insisted there could be no role for European powers at the meeting.

"France will be there and will ensure that Europe's voice is heard," Jean-Noël Barrot told French radio. He did not say who would represent Paris, or whether French or other European officials would take part directly in negotiations, or simply observe.

The meetings, which are set to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, had previously been presented as a three-way session between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv.

The Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had earlier ruled out a European role, saying the trilateral format had already been agreed.

Talking to a Russian news channel on Friday, he accused European governments of failing to decide who speaks for them, while acknowledging that security talks would at some point require Europe's involvement.

On Thursday, President Trump met Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and said a coming agreement was "going to involve more than Ukraine," adding he could even say it "might involve all of Europe."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told CNN on Friday that he had not been given details of the agreement Trump had referenced, and warned: "For me, it's not simple, and it can be dangerous." He invoked the 1945 Yalta conference, where Allied leaders settled Europe's division without the involvement of several affected countries.

This will be the fourth round of talks between the two warring nations brokered by the Trump administration, and the first since those in Geneva this February. Earlier U.S.-brokered meetings have made little progress, and the chances of a breakthrough have been reduced as the Trump administration focused on its war with Iran.

Moscow confirmed it would return to the negotiating table only following a visit by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg in October. Those talks saw Putin announce the release of an American prisoner from a Russian jail — an apparent Kremlin gesture to President Trump's earlier lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Ukraine was vehemently opposed to the fuel sales — arguing they helped replenish Moscow's war chest.

Witkoff has said the agenda for these latest talks will include postwar security arrangements and de-escalation of the conflict and humanitarian issues, shortly after Melania Trump helped broker a limited ceasefire that allowed humanitarian aid to enter a town inside Russian-occupied Ukraine.

Russia's delegation will again be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a hardline Putin aide who has participated in most talks with Ukraine since the unsuccessful first set of discussions all the way back in March 2022.

For the first time, these talks will also include Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as Yury Zhigarlovsky, a deputy head of the General Staff's operations directorate, alongside military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

This more senior lineup could indicate that Moscow is readier than before to address thorny political and military questions. But the U.S. think tankInstitute for the Study of War suggested some of those same Russian officials have in fact previously sought to slow down previous talks or push harder on Moscow's demands.

The gaps between the two countries remain substantial. Russia has demanded that Ukraine give up large parts of its territory and renounce NATO membership. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted any security commitments should be clearly spelled out, including who would act, and how, if Russia attacked again.

Some analysts expect little. In an op-ed for the Atlantic Council think tank, the former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine John Herbst argued that Putin had rejected every U.S. proposal Kyiv accepted and preferred participating in peace talks than pursuing actual peace. "Perhaps the only outcome of the talks," he wrote, "will be to agree to another round."

The meetings in the United Arab Emirates also follow Democrats' midterm victories, which Zelenskyy said could improve Ukraine's chances of more U.S. aid.

Russia, too, may be looking to push for the Trump administration's outlines of a Ukraine deal — before a Democratic-controlled Congress arrives come January.

Also hovering over the talks — the prospect of Trump, Xi, and Putin gathering for a trilateral meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China later this month. While details remain murky, all sides have confirmed discussions are underway.

And as officials travel to Abu Dhabi to talk peace, the war has raged on regardless.

Zelenskyy said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at the Kyiv area overnight Saturday, with only four intercepted, accusing Moscow of treating diplomacy "as a form of aggression."

In southern Ukraine, the death toll from a guided-bomb strike Monday on an aid distribution site in Komyshuvakha rose to at least 55.
